title: Auto Shut-Off Electric Kettles: Three Hamilton Beach Models Under $35
subtitle: What automatic shutoff does and does not do, and what to check before buying one of three Hamilton Beach kettles priced at $35 or less.
excerpt: An electric kettle with automatic shutoff heats water on its own base and stops heating at the boil. Here is what it can and cannot do, and three Hamilton Beach models under $35.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: For many of us, the morning cup of tea or instant coffee starts with a stovetop kettle. That means lifting a metal pot to the sink, carrying it to the burner and remembering to come back before it boils dry. If your hands or wrists ache, each of those steps can be a small struggle.

An electric kettle with automatic shutoff takes the burner out of the picture. It heats water on its own base and stops heating when the water boils. That means fewer steps and less to remember. One caution up front: this article covers only Hamilton Beach kettles, using the maker's own product pages. We did not compare other brands, and we did not find independent reviews to draw on.
How an auto shut-off kettle works

The kettle sits on a flat base that plugs into the wall. You fill the kettle, set it on the base and flip a switch. On the 1.7-liter black model (41038G) and the 1-liter model (40998), Hamilton Beach describes an illuminated on/off switch. On the black model, the light stays on while heating and goes off at the boil. The glass model (40864G) has a plain on/off switch and a soft blue light while heating; its page does not describe how the switch behaves at the boil.

Two more features appear on these pages. Boil-dry protection is meant to shut the kettle off if there is no water in it. Cord-free serving is Hamilton Beach's term for lifting the kettle off its base to pour. The 41038G page makes this claim, and the notes say the cord is short, so you need counter space near an outlet.
"Built-in safety features like automatic shutoff and boil-dry protection make it safer than boiling a kettle on the stovetop." (Hamilton Beach, product page for the 1.7 Liter Glass Electric Kettle)

That is the maker's own claim about its glass model, not an independent finding. It helps to be clear about what a kettle cannot do. Automatic shutoff stops the heating; it does not make the water safe to touch. What comes out is still boiling hot and can scald if it spills. A kettle also does not replace a stove auto shut-off device or other fire-safety gear.

One more point for readers with stiff hands or weak grip. None of the three kettles has been checked for grip or ease of use. The pages do not state the empty weight, the handle type or how much force the lid needs. Please look at these in a store if you can.

items: Size versus weight. Shipping weights run about 1.8 to 2.6 pounds, and a full 1.7-liter kettle adds roughly 3.7 pounds of water. The 1-liter model is lighter to lift but holds less. You can also fill only as much as you need.
A simple switch. Fewer controls mean fewer things to learn. The black 41038G uses one flip-down switch near the base.
The lid. The 40998 has a push-button lid. The pages do not say how much force any lid needs, so test it in a store if you can.
The handle. The pages do not describe handle type. If possible, hold a display model and see how it feels in your hand.
A water window. The 40998 and 41038G have a water-level window, and the glass model lets you see inside.
Counter space. The cord is short, so the kettle needs room near an outlet.

Replacement parts and cleaning. Hamilton Beach's site lists a replacement base at $21.99 and a filter at $5.99 for the 40998 (November 2026). Scale buildup from minerals in water needs occasional descaling, and the glass model has a wide opening for easier cleaning.
Returns. As general advice, check the store's return policy before you buy.

sections.content: Setting it up and using it well
Choose a flat, dry spot on the counter near an outlet. Hamilton Beach sums up the 1.7-liter black model's routine in one line: "Simply fill with water and flip down the on/off switch near the base."

Set your mug on the counter right beside the kettle so you are not carrying boiling water across the kitchen. Pour slowly, keep your hand clear of the steam and set the kettle back on its base when you are done. Glass can break if dropped, so handle the glass model with care.

An electric kettle still produces boiling water, and the notes advise it is not suited to people with a tremor or cognitive decline who might leave it on a hot base or pour unsafely. If that describes someone in your household, ask their doctor what is safest. This is not a medical or safety guarantee.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: An electric kettle does one job: it boils water and then stops heating. Since we looked at only one brand, consider this a starting point. If you can, try lifting a kettle in a store first, then choose the size that feels right in your hands.

products.name: Hamilton Beach 1 Liter Stainless Steel Electric Kettle (model 40998)
products.blurb: The smallest of the three, and lighter to lift because it holds less. It has a push-button lid, an illuminated on/off switch, a water-level window and auto shutoff with boil-dry protection.

products.name: Hamilton Beach 1.7 Liter Electric Kettle, Black (model 41038G)
products.blurb: Suits anyone who wants a larger kettle with one flip-down switch near the base; the switch light goes off at the boil. It is 1500 watts, with a water window, boil-dry protection and a BPA-free interior.

products.name: Hamilton Beach 1.7 Liter Glass Electric Kettle (model 40864G)
products.blurb: For anyone who likes to see inside, with glass sides and a soft blue light while heating. It has a wide opening for easier cleaning, though glass can break if dropped.
